title: Merging streams and the median
sub: A heap of the heads of k lists in O(N log k), two heaps for a streaming median, and the median frame time in Unity
cards/0/body:
Merge k Sorted Lists (LeetCode #23, hard). Given an array of k linked lists, each sorted in ascending order, merge them into one sorted list and return its head. Constraints: 0 ≤ k ≤ 10⁴, up to 500 nodes per list, N ≤ 10⁴ nodes in total, values up to 10⁴ in absolute value. Empty lists and an empty array are valid input.

Signals for a heap of heads:

1. You have k already ordered sequences and need the overall order.
2. At every step you need the minimum of k candidates — one from each sequence — and once chosen, a candidate is replaced by the next one from the same sequence.

This is signal 2 from the first lesson — “the minimum of a changing set, again and again” — except the set is the heads of the lists. In real life this is how sorted chunks are merged in an external sort of files, how logs from several servers are merged by time, how replay records from several clients are combined.
cards/1/q: Where does a heap of the heads of k sequences work? Select all.
cards/1/options/0: Merge 50 server logs, each sorted by time, into one
cards/1/options/1: The k-th smallest element of an n×n matrix in which every row is sorted
cards/1/options/2: The median of an unsorted array
cards/1/options/3: The longest substring without repeating characters
cards/1/explain: The logs are exactly Merge k Sorted Lists. The matrix is the same n sorted sequences: the heap holds the row heads, you take the minimum k times and push the next element of the same row (that is #378). The median of an unsorted array is quickselect: there are no ordered pieces there. A substring without repeats is a sliding window: there is one sequence there, not k.
cards/2/body:
Collect everything and sort: O(N log N) time and O(N) memory for the array of values. It works, but it ignores the fact that the lists are already sorted, and it does not suit streams that do not fit in memory.

Merge one at a time: result ← merge(result, next list). Merging two is two pointers plus a dummy head dummy: it always has a tail to append to, so the first node needs no special case; the answer is dummy.next. The trouble is that the result grows and is walked again every time. Say there are k lists of n nodes: the merges cost 2n + 3n + … + kn ≈ k²n / 2 = N·k / 2.

Pairwise (divide and conquer): merge the lists in pairs, then pairs of pairs. There are log₂ k levels, each touching N nodes in total — O(N log k), like the heap, and with no extra memory if you merge in place.
cards/3/q: k = 1000 lists of 100 nodes, N = 10⁵. How many steps does merging one at a time take, and how many does the heap of heads take?
cards/3/options/1: ≈ 10⁵ and ≈ 10⁵: both visit each node once
cards/3/explain: One at a time: N·k / 2 = 10⁵ · 1000 / 2 = 5·10⁷ — the early nodes are walked again in every later merge. The heap: N nodes, each one insertion and one removal at O(log k), log₂ 1000 ≈ 10, about 10⁶ in total. The difference is 50×, and it grows with k.
cards/3/wrong/1: Only the heap (and pairwise merging, per level) visits each node once. When merging one at a time, the first lists are walked in each of the k merges.
cards/3/wrong/2: 10⁸ is N·k without dividing by 2, and 1.7·10⁶ is N log N, the cost of sorting everything. A heap of k heads costs N log k.
cards/4/title: The idea: a heap of heads
cards/4/body:
The minimum of everything that remains is among the heads of the lists: each list is sorted, so its head is its minimum. It is therefore enough to keep one head from each non-empty list in a min-heap (the priority is the node’s value).

Step: take the smallest head, append it to the answer, push its next into the heap if there is one. A list that runs out simply drops out: the heap shrinks.

Invariant: the heap holds exactly one node from each non-empty list — the first one not yet taken. So the root is the minimum of everything that remains, and the answer grows in ascending order.

Cost: N nodes, each entering and leaving the heap once — O(N log k) time and O(k) memory, not O(N): nodes are not copied, we only relink next.

Equal values. PriorityQueue is not stable, and of two heads with the same value either may come out first. For numbers that does not matter. If you merge events by time and need source order for equal times, use the priority (time, listIndex).
cards/4/flow/0: push the head of each list
cards/4/deep:
Pairwise merging versus the heap. Both are O(N log k). Pairwise merging allocates nothing and needs no heap, but it requires all lists to be at hand. The heap works with streams: it only needs the current head of each source, which is why sorted chunks on disk are merged this way in an external sort — memory holds k heads and read buffers, not N records.

Merging enumerators. The same code works on IEnumerator<T> instead of nodes: the heap holds an enumerator with its Current as priority; after yielding, call MoveNext(), and if it returns true, the enumerator goes back into the heap. The result can be produced with yield return — lazily, one element at a time.

Stability. If, for equal keys, the element from the lower-numbered list must come first, the priority is the tuple (value, listIndex): a tuple compares field by field, and no equal priorities remain. Within one source stability holds by itself — its elements enter the heap one at a time, the next only after the previous one.

Allocations. PriorityQueue<ListNode, int> keeps the pairs in a single array: once it has grown to k, there are no new allocations. Set the capacity in the constructor — new PriorityQueue<ListNode, int>(lists.Length) — and there will be no growth either.
cards/5/q: Assemble the merge of k lists with a heap of heads.
cards/5/explain: The priority is the node’s value, so the min-heap yields the smallest head; with −node.val the list would come out in descending order. The tail moves to the node just appended. The heap receives the next node of the same list, if there is one — that keeps the invariant “one head from each non-empty list”. The answer is dummy.next: dummy itself is a placeholder node with value 0.
cards/6/task: Step through the trace on L1 = [1, 4, 5], L2 = [1, 3, 4], L3 = [2, 6]. The rig asks twice what the code will do: track which list each head came from.
cards/6/goal/asks/0/options/0/label: Takes 3 from L2 and pushes the next node of L2 — 4
cards/6/goal/asks/0/options/1/label: Takes 3 from L2 and pushes the next node of L3 — 6
cards/6/goal/asks/0/options/2/label: Takes 4 from L1: that head has been in the heap the longest
cards/6/goal/asks/0/q: The answer already has 1, 1, 2. The heap holds the heads 3 (L2), 4 (L1), 6 (L3). What does the code do?
cards/6/goal/asks/0/explain: The root is the smallest head, 3 from L2. After it, the next node of the same list goes into the heap, 4 from L2 — the invariant “one head from each list”. How long a head has been sitting in the heap does not matter: only the value decides.
cards/6/goal/asks/1/options/0/label: Takes 4 from L2 and pushes nothing: 5 and 6 remain in the heap
cards/6/goal/asks/1/options/1/label: Takes 4 from L2 and pushes null into the heap
cards/6/goal/asks/1/options/2/label: Stops: one of the lists has ended
cards/6/goal/asks/1/q: The heap holds 4 (L2), 6 (L3), 5 (L1). L2 has no nodes after the 4. What does the code do?
cards/6/goal/asks/1/explain: The minimum is 4 from L2, and it gets appended. node.next == null, and the check before Enqueue lets nothing into the heap: L2 simply drops out, and the heap shrinks to two heads, 5 and 6. The loop runs while the heap is non-empty, not while all lists are alive.
cards/7/body:
Find Median from Data Stream (LeetCode #295, hard). The class MedianFinder: AddNum(x) adds a number, FindMedian() returns the median of everything added — the middle element or the mean of the two middle ones. Numbers range from −10⁵ to 10⁵, up to 5·10⁴ calls.

Naively: keep a sorted List<int> and insert with BinarySearch + Insert — the search is O(log n), but the insertion shifts the tail, O(n). In the worst case 5·10⁴ calls make n²/2 ≈ 1.25·10⁹ shifts: a shift is a fast memmove, but the growth is quadratic.

The idea: the median does not need the whole order — only the boundary between the smaller and the larger half. Split the numbers into two heaps: low is a max-heap of the smaller half (priority −x, safe since |x| ≤ 10⁵), high is a min-heap of the larger half. The roots face each other across the boundary.

Invariant: (1) everything in low ≤ everything in high; (2) |low| = |high| or |low| = |high| + 1. Then the median is the root of low for an odd count, or the mean of the two roots for an even count.

AddNum: put x into low if it is not greater than its root, otherwise into high — that keeps (1). Then, if the sizes have drifted apart, move one root to the other heap — that keeps (2). Adding is O(log n), the median is O(1). In Unity, use two MinHeap<int> from the first lesson of the unit, with a descending comparer for low.
cards/8/task: Step through the trace on the stream 5, 15, 1, 3, 8, 7, 9, 10. The rig asks twice what AddNum will do: check both parts of the invariant.
cards/8/goal/asks/0/options/0/label: 3 → low; low is two larger than high — 5 moves to high; the median is 4
cards/8/goal/asks/0/options/2/label: 3 → high, because high has fewer elements
cards/8/goal/asks/0/q: 3 has arrived. low = {1, 5}, high = {15}. What does AddNum do?
cards/8/goal/asks/0/explain: 3 ≤ 5 (the root of low), so it goes into low — otherwise “low ≤ high” would break. Now low has three numbers and high has one: a difference of two, so the root of low, 5, moves to high. low = {1, 3}, high = {5, 15} — equal sizes, and the median is the mean of the roots, (3 + 5) / 2 = 4. Where to put a number is decided by its value, not by the sizes: the second step evens the sizes out.
cards/8/goal/asks/1/q: 9 has arrived. low = {1, 3, 5}, high = {7, 8, 15}. What will the median be?
cards/8/goal/asks/1/explain: 9 > 5, so it goes into high, which now has four against three. The root of high, 7, moves to low: low = {1, 3, 5, 7}, high = {8, 9, 15}. Seven elements, an odd count — the median is the root of low, 7. Check: in order 1, 3, 5, 7, 8, 9, 15, the middle is 7.
cards/9/q: After AddNum(1) and AddNum(2) this FindMedian returns 1 instead of 1.5. Tap the line with the bug.
cards/9/explain: Peek returns an int, the sum is an int, and dividing by 2 is integer division: 3 / 2 = 1. Only the result is converted to double. You need / 2.0 — then the sum is converted to double before the division. There is no overflow here: |x| ≤ 10⁵, but with values near int.MaxValue the sum of the two roots would have to be computed in long.
cards/10/body:
A HUD or telemetry needs a “typical frame time”. The mean is dragged up by spikes — garbage collection, shader compilation, scene loading: 119 frames of 16 ms and one of 500 ms give a mean of 20 ms but a median of 16. That is why you show the median, and the spikes separately: p99 or the maximum.

A window of the last N frames. The two heaps of #295 accumulate everything from the start, while here an old frame has to leave. PriorityQueue cannot remove (Remove only since .NET 9, and in O(n)), and Unity does not have it at all. What people do:

1. N ≈ 120 — copy and sort. A ring buffer of N values; on request, copy into a preallocated array and call Array.Sort: about 120 · 7 ≈ 840 comparisons, a few microseconds, no new arrays.
2. A narrow range — counters. Frame times from 0 to 100 ms in 0.1 ms steps are 1000 counter buckets: adding and removing are O(1), a percentile is a walk over the buckets. This is the #295 follow-up: “all numbers are from 0 to 100” → an array of 101 counters.
3. A large window and an exact median — Sliding Window Median (#480): two heaps with lazy deletion. Do not search for the leaving element; record “delete x” in a dictionary, and when x reaches a root, remove it. Count the sizes of the halves by live elements only. Or two SortedSet<(int value, int index)>: the index keeps equal values from collapsing into one.
cards/10/deep:
Lazy deletion in detail. It is the same trick as in Dijkstra on PriorityQueue instead of decrease-key: the stale entry stays in the heap and is recognized and skipped when it comes out. For a window median: a dictionary delayed “value → how many copies to delete”; when an element leaves the window, delayed[x]++ and adjust the live-element counter of the half where x lives (compare with the root of low). After every operation, “clean” the roots: while a root is in delayed, pop it and decrement the counter. The heap may bloat with dead elements, but each one is physically removed once — amortized O(log n) per step.

Why not UnorderedItems. PriorityQueue has the UnorderedItems enumeration, but it goes in the order of the internal array — fine for debugging, and for finding an element it is still O(n).

SortedSet instead of heaps. Two SortedSet<(int value, int index)> give O(log n) removal directly, with no dead elements, while Max and Min walk down to the extreme node. The price is a tree node on the managed heap for every insertion: in Unity that is garbage every frame, so lazy heaps on arrays or counters are the better deal.

A percentile from counters. For the p-th percentile, walk the buckets accumulating a sum and stop once it exceeds p · count. The precision is the bucket width; spikes above 100 ms go into the last bucket, and the maximum is shown separately.
cards/11/q: A #295 follow-up: every number in the stream is an integer from 0 to 100. How do you speed up MedianFinder?
cards/11/options/0: An array of 101 counters: AddNum is O(1), FindMedian is a walk over 101 buckets
cards/11/options/1: You cannot: two heaps already give O(log n) and O(1)
cards/11/options/2: A sorted List<int> with BinarySearch: insertion in O(log n)
cards/11/explain: The values are small integers in a known range, like the frequencies in the buckets of the previous lesson: no comparisons needed, counting is enough. Adding is count[x]++, the median is a walk over the buckets until the sum reaches the middle: 101 steps, independent of n, and no heaps at all.
cards/11/wrong/1: Two heaps are good for arbitrary numbers. When the range is 101 values, counters give O(1) per addition and a constant for the median, without a single heap.
cards/11/wrong/2: BinarySearch finds the position in O(log n), but Insert shifts the tail of the list — O(n) per insertion. That is the naive solution from the card on two heaps.
cards/12/q: You are solving Find Median from Data Stream out loud. Put the steps in order.
cards/12/items/0: Clarify: how many AddNum and FindMedian calls, the range of the numbers, what to return for an even count
cards/12/items/1: Naively: a sorted list with insertion — O(n) per AddNum
cards/12/items/2: Idea: the median is the boundary between halves; low is a max-heap of the smaller half, high a min-heap of the larger
cards/12/items/3: Invariant: low ≤ high and |low| − |high| is 0 or 1
cards/12/items/4: Write AddNum: place by value, then even out the sizes with one move
cards/12/items/5: Run 5, 15, 1, 3 and show 5 moving to high
cards/12/items/6: Complexity: AddNum O(log n), FindMedian O(1), memory O(n); the follow-up on the range 0–100 means counters
cards/12/explain: Asking about an even count and the range fixes both the answer type (double) and the likely follow-up. The invariant is stated before the code — it shows why AddNum has two steps: the first keeps the halves ordered, the second keeps their sizes.
